newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, Japan criticize reporters in hostage deadlock.
newsitem.headline: Peru, Japan criticize reporters in hostage deadlock.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis entered its 22nd day on Wednesday with the Peruvian and Japanese governments criticising reporters for jeopardising efforts to end the standoff, in which Marxist rebels held 74 hostages.

Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, speaking on a tour of Southeast Asian nations, on Wednesday criticised a Japanese journalist for entering the besieged residence of his country's ambassador in Lima, saying he could have harmed efforts to solve the crisis.
"It is very regrettable," a Foreign Ministry official quoted Hashimoto as telling reporters travelling with him.
"An act like that could create unforeseeable circumstances and disrupt the Peruvian government's efforts for a peaceful resolution and the release of all hostages," he said.

A Japanese reporter for a subsidiary of Japanese television station TV Asahi and his interpreter entered the residence on Tuesday at the invitation of the rebels of Peru's Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) after sneaking through a private house to get past Peruvian police.
They left about two hours later, only to be arrested and driven away by anti-terrorism police to their headquarters in downtown Lima, where their notebooks and camera were confiscated.
TV Asahi named the two as Peruvian interpreter Victor Borja and New York-based reporter Tsuyoshi Hitomi. As of Wednesday morning there had been no report of their release.

Their entry into the residence, as well as that on New Year's Eve by a bigger group of journalists, was also condemned by Peruvian Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi as "damaging to the seriousness and fluidity of talks."
A spokesman for TV Asahi said the company did not instruct the reporter to enter the residence and his supervisor in Lima was not aware of Hitomi's attempts, Kyodo news agency reported.

The MRTA rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17 and took about 500 hostages including ambassadors and senior Peruvian government officials. Most of them were later released, leaving 74 hostages remaining.

Peru's President Alberto Fujimori on Tuesday decried "terrorist blackmail" by the guerrillas but his government said it would continue contact with the rebels to try and end the standoff without bloodshed.
"We maintain a firm position of not giving in to blackmail from the terrorists," Fujimori told reporters during a surprise visit to a Lima shantytown.
He said he hoped for a peaceful solution to the crisis and said the "physical well-being" of the hostages was assured "because there are not going to be acts of blood."
His prime minister, Pandolfi, said later that the government would continue "unofficial dealings" with the rebels.
"The council of ministers has agreed to continue, in a timely way, the unofficial dealings towards reaching a global solution to the problem," Pandolfi said in a statement.

He said these dealings -- led so far by Education Minister Domingo Palermo -- were aimed at "exhausting all possible means for achieving a peaceful solution guaranteeing the physical integrity of those people kidnapped in the residence of the Japanese ambassador."

He did not say when Palermo would return to the residence, where he has not been seen for more than a week. His absence had prompted the rebels to say initial talks had been broken off by the government.

Fujimori, who had ended his regular visits to shantytowns when the crisis began, said his trip was intended to show the world that life continued as normal in Peru despite the MRTA's takeover of the residence. "We should not transmit the image that in Peru we are living a situation of terrorism," he said.
The rebels are demanding the release of some 400 colleagues from Peruvian prisons. Fujimori has said he will not do this.
